newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH LEGISLATORS MOVE TO ADOPT NEW CONSTITUTION.
newsitem.headline: POLISH LEGISLATORS MOVE TO ADOPT NEW CONSTITUTION.

text.p: Polish legislators moved closer on Friday to approve the country's new constitution, which would replace a communist-era charter, by setting a date for the document's second reading next month, PAP news agency said.
It quoted parliamentary speaker Jozef Zych as saying that senior deputies of parliament's two houses agreed to begin the reading on February 24.

This would pave the way for staging a national referendum on the constitution in May as suggested by President Aleksander Kwasniewski and four biggest parties present in parliament, which have been working on the draft for the last three years.
Kwasniewski has said he is unlikely to propose any major changes to the document and will promptly submit it to the third and final reading so that the May referendum deadline is met.
If the constitution is not approved before general elections due in September or October, different parties might win the polls and work on the draft would begin afresh.

The rightist, Catholic parties, which were so split that they failed to enter parliament in 1993 elections and therefore had little say on the draft, reject its secular tone and want the charter to be founded on religious ideas of "natural law".
These parties, notably a strong new alliance around the Solidarity trade union, plan to oppose the current draft during the referendum or maybe change it if they win the elections.
This would extend a process which has dragged on embarrassingly long after the 1989 fall of communism, leaving Poland's system based on an interim "small" constitution.
But Zych said parliamentarians would meet Solidarity representatives next week to hammer out a compromise.

The new constitution guarantees free publicly funded basic health care for all regardless of income and free education, although the draft admits the possibility of some charges for higher state education.
The presidency would be slightly weakened, with parliament allowed to overthrow the president's veto by three-fifths of votes in the lower house rather than the present two-thirds majority.
The president would also have less say on appointments in the foreign, defense and interior ministries.
